name: Straightening hair brush

angle.text: A heated brush straightens and smooths hair while brushing, giving a sleeker style that is visible straight away and lasts until the next wash. It uses the same heat principle as a flat iron and has no dedicated research.

summary: Heated paddle brush that straightens as you brush; same heat mechanism as a flat iron, with no dedicated research.
note: No studies specific to straightening brushes; general heat-damage cautions apply.
currentQuick:
A straightening brush is a heated paddle brush that straightens hair as it is brushed through, a hybrid of a hairbrush and a flat iron. The first brand-name version, DAFNI, was released in 2015 after a ceramic design was patented in 2013.
No dedicated studies of these brushes were found.
How it works: Heat reshapes hydrogen bonds in the hair so it can be held straight, as with a flat iron; the bonds can re-form with moisture.
Risks and caveats: Overuse of heated styling tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot surfaces can burn skin.
deepLead:
A straightening hair brush is a heated paddle-style brush that straightens hair as the user brushes through it, combining the surface of a hairbrush with the heated plates of a flat iron. According to Wikipedia, a ceramic straightening brush was patented in 2013, and Sharon Rabi released the first one under the DAFNI brand in 2015 .
The tool has a larger heated surface than a traditional flat iron . No published clinical studies of straightening brushes were found; the underlying heat-straightening mechanism is the same as for flat irons, which work by breaking hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex, with bonds able to re-form when hair is exposed to moisture, and which can cause damage when overused .

name: Flat iron / hair straightener

angle.text: Users clamp hair with a flat iron to straighten curls or add waves, producing a styled look that is visible immediately and lasts until the next wash. The styling effect is plainly observable, and heat damage is covered in the article.

summary: Heated clamp plates that straighten or wave hair; the effect is real but temporary and heat damage and burns are the documented downsides.
note: Overuse of heat can damage hair; plates can cause contact burns.
currentQuick:
A flat iron uses two heated plates to straighten curly or wavy hair, and can also be used to add waves. It is a standard styling tool and its basic effect is well established.
The straightened shape is not permanent in the same way as chemical treatments: encyclopedic sources say moisture can restore the original shape, although repeated high-heat ironing has been shown in a lab study to straighten curly hair irreversibly.
How it works: Heat lets hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex be reshaped while the hair is held straight; they can re-form when the hair gets damp.
Risks and caveats: Overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot plates can cause contact burns, including in children. Large studies linking hair straighteners to cancers or fibroids mostly concern chemical relaxers rather than heat tools.
deepLead:
A flat iron, also called a hair straightener, is a heated styling tool with two plates that clamp and glide along sections of hair to straighten or reshape them. It is used to smooth curly or wavy hair, and also to add bends or loose waves .
According to Wikipedia, heat straightening works by breaking hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex, which can re-form when the hair is exposed to moisture, and overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage . A laboratory study with an automated iron found that repeated ironing at temperatures from 120 to 175 degrees Celsius produced irreversible straightening in curly hair, with a role for silicone products in the process . Published safety research on flat irons themselves concerns mainly burns; larger epidemiological studies of hair straightening concern chemical relaxers rather than heated irons .

name: Hair dryer brush / hot air brush

angle.text: A hot air brush dries and styles hair in one pass, giving volume and a smooth blowout that is visible right away. Claims come from product reviews and the effect is observable without clinical studies.

summary: Brush-dryer hybrid for volume and quick blowouts; claims come from product reviews, with no clinical studies.
note: Sources are consumer reviews; no clinical studies on volume or hair damage.
currentQuick:
A hot air brush is a brush with heated airflow built in, so hair is dried and styled at once. It is promoted for root lift and volume, especially on fine hair.
The claims come from product testers, and no clinical studies were found.
How it works: A motor blows heated air through the brush head while bristles lift and shape hair, drying and smoothing it in one step.
Risks and caveats: No device-specific safety research was found; the main consideration is heat exposure to hair and scalp, as with other heated styling tools.
deepLead:
A hot air brush, also called a hair dryer brush or blow-dry brush, is a handheld styling tool that combines a brush with heated airflow so that hair can be dried, smoothed and given volume in one pass. Models such as the Revlon One-Step are commonly named examples .
Descriptions of the tool come mainly from consumer-review-style sources rather than clinical research. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia that cites product testers, says hot air brushes are particularly used for root lift and body on fine hair, and that testers report faster drying than a separate dryer and round brush . No published clinical studies of hot air brushes were found.

name: Premium multi-styler

angle.text: Users buy multi-stylers such as the Dyson Airwrap to dry, curl, smooth and add volume with one device, for a styled look that is visible immediately. Manufacturer claims about gentler styling are untested in published studies.

summary: A pricey multi-attachment styling tool from Dyson and rivals; its benefits are claimed by makers but untested in published studies.
note: Styling effects are cosmetic and last until the next wash; no independent trials found.
currentQuick:
A premium multi-styler is a hair tool with swappable heads that can dry, curl, smooth and add volume. The best-known example is the Dyson Airwrap, and several competitors now sell similar devices.
It is a styling aid, not a treatment: any change to the look of the hair lasts only until the hair is next washed or restyled.
How it works: The device blows heated air through attachments that wrap, brush or shape the hair. Makers say airflow lets them style at lower heat than traditional irons; this is a manufacturer claim and no independent trial was found.
Risks and caveats: As with other heated tools, burns and heat-related hair damage are possible. No medical regulation applies to it as a consumer appliance. Rival makers have been involved in patent disputes with Dyson.
deepLead:
A premium multi-styler is a high-priced, multi-attachment hair tool that combines drying, curling, smoothing and volumising functions in one device. The category is most closely associated with the Dyson Airwrap, made by the British appliance company Dyson, which also sells hair dryers and other styling tools. Competing products from other manufacturers have followed, and Dyson has taken legal action against at least one rival over patents covering an air-styling device.
The tools are discussed as a way to shape hair with less direct heat contact than a conventional curling iron or flat iron, using airflow and interchangeable attachments. Manufacturers make this claim about their own designs; no published clinical trial of a multi-styler's effect on hair condition, styling outcome or attractiveness for this article.
Because the sources for this entry are thin, the article is brief. It covers the product category, its commercial context and what is and is not known about its effects.

name: Wig (lace front)

chain: Hair covers thin or bald areas
angle.text: A lace front wig gives a full head of hair with a hairline that appears to grow from the skin, so the change is visible the moment it is worn. It is removable and has not been tested in trials.

summary: A hand-tied lace hairline wig that instantly covers hair loss; the effect is removable and no trials have tested it.
note: No trials of lace fronts; attachment methods may strain the scalp.
currentQuick:
A lace front wig has a thin skin-toned mesh at the front with hairs tied in by hand, so the hairline looks natural. It is used for fashion and to conceal hair loss, including medical hair loss.
It works only while worn, and no trial has tested lace fronts specifically.
How it works: The lace foundation blends with the skin at the hairline, and the hair is attached by pins, elastic or skin-safe adhesive.
Risks and caveats: Adhesives and tight attachment can irritate the scalp. Cost and replacement needs vary with materials. Wigs are not regulated as drugs.
deepLead:
A lace front wig is a wig whose front hairline is made from a fine, skin-coloured mesh, usually called hair lace, into which individual hairs are tied by hand so that the hairline appears to grow from the skin. The base is commonly made of French or Swiss lace, and full-lace and partial-lace versions also exist.
Wigs in general are worn for fashion, theatre, protection of natural hair and convenience, and by people with medical hair loss, most often those undergoing chemotherapy or living with alopecia areata. In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, lace fronts are discussed mainly as a concealment option for hairline loss.
No clinical trial specific to lace front wigs is available. The cosmetic effect is immediate and removable, and the main documented considerations are cost, upkeep, and the effects of attachment methods on the scalp.

name: Hair system / toupee

angle.text: Men with hair loss use custom hair systems, attached with adhesive or tape, to restore a full hairline and density while worn, a change that is visible immediately. Trials are absent; the scalp-massage hairline claim is untested and based on anecdote.

summary: A custom non-surgical hairpiece for balding men; it covers hair loss while worn, with no trials and documented traction hair loss in some wearers.
note: Adhesive and weave attachments are linked to traction-type hair loss in case reports.
currentQuick:
A hair system is a custom-made hairpiece, usually attached with adhesive or tape, that covers or fills in areas of hair loss. Toupees have been sold for more than a century and remain one option alongside drugs, transplants and shaving the head.
It is a camouflage rather than a treatment: appearance changes only while it is worn, and no trial has measured its effect.
How it works: A base of fine lace or similar material carries natural or synthetic hair and is fixed to the scalp by adhesive, elastic or by weaving it into existing hair.
Risks and caveats: A 2024 case series reported hair loss in six hair system wearers, and weaving methods are linked to traction alopecia. Pieces need regular replacement and care; saltwater, chlorine and some shampoos damage fibres.
deepLead:
A toupee is a hairpiece or partial wig of natural or synthetic hair worn to cover partial baldness or for theatrical purposes; the word comes from the French toupet, meaning a tuft of hair. In modern hair-loss communities the term hair system usually refers to a custom-made, non-surgical hair prosthesis, typically fixed to the scalp with adhesive or tape, that replaces or fills in lost hair.
Dermatology literature lists hairpieces among the hair camouflage options available when medical and surgical treatments are insufficient or unsuitable. A 2024 case series of six patients examined hair system-induced alopecia, asking whether it arises from traction or from pressure. No trial has compared hair systems with other treatments for appearance or quality of life.
On looksmaxxing forums, hair systems are discussed as one of several routes for men with hair loss, alongside drug treatment, transplantation and a shaved head.

name: Electric shaver (foil/rotary)

angle.text: Users shave with foil or rotary electric shavers for a clean, tidy face or body, with less redness than blades according to mostly manufacturer research. The shaved result is visible immediately.

summary: A motorised shaver with foil or rotary heads, offered as a lower-irritation alternative to blades; comfort claims come mostly from manufacturer research.
note: Rare contact-allergy case reports (nickel, fragrance); little independent comparative research.
currentQuick:
An electric shaver cuts hair with moving blades under a perforated foil or rotary head, so the blades do not touch the skin directly. Foil models are often described as closer-cutting; rotary models suit some face shapes and beards better, according to user preference.
It is a grooming tool, and its results last only until hair regrows. Research on skin comfort is mostly from the cosmetic industry.
How it works: A motor oscillates or rotates cutters behind a guard; hairs enter holes or slots and are sheared against the guard.
Risks and caveats: Irritation is possible, and case reports describe contact allergy to nickel or fragrance components in shavers. Skin often needs time to adjust to electric shaving.
deepLead:
An electric shaver, also called an electric razor, is a handheld grooming device in which a motor drives oscillating or rotating blades behind a protective perforated guard, cutting facial or body hair without direct blade contact with the skin. The two main designs are foil shavers, which use a thin perforated foil over oscillating cutters, and rotary shavers, which use rotating cutting heads.
Electric shaving is commonly offered as an alternative to blade razors for people who find wet shaving irritating, although published sources describe skin comfort as something manufacturers have had to balance against how closely the device cuts. A 2016 review from the cosmetic science literature describes research aimed at reducing electric-shaving-induced skin irritation.
No randomised clinical trial comparing electric shavers with blade razors for appearance outcomes.

name: Cartridge razor

angle.text: The cartridge razor is the standard tool for a close, clean shave, with the result visible right after. One 59-man study found more redness than with a safety razor.

summary: The standard multi-blade razor with a disposable head; one 59-man study found it left more redness than a safety razor.
note: Single comparison study (cartridge vs safety razor); proprietary cartridges tie buyers to a brand.
currentQuick:
A cartridge razor clips a disposable multi-blade head onto a handle. It has been the dominant style of razor since the 1970s, and makers have steadily added more blades.
It is a grooming tool with no lasting effect on appearance. The main published comparison found more redness than with a safety razor.
How it works: Several blades set in a row in the cartridge cut the hair in successive passes; the cartridge snaps off when dull.
Risks and caveats: Razor-related redness and irritation were higher with a three-blade cartridge than a safety razor in one 2024 study of 59 men. Cuts are possible with any razor.
deepLead:
A cartridge razor is a manual razor whose blades, typically two to six or more, are mounted in a disposable plastic cartridge that clips onto a reusable handle. Cartridge and disposable razors have been the predominant type of razor since the 1970s.
The design was introduced commercially in 1970 by Wilkinson, whose Bonded Shaving System embedded a single blade in a disposable cartridge, and Gillette answered in 1971 with the twin-blade Trac II. Manufacturers have since added blades, and market commentary and Wikipedia note that multi-blade cartridges carry high profit margins and tie buyers to proprietary cartridges.
One 2024 study in 59 men compared a cartridge razor with a safety razor and found more shaving-induced redness with the cartridge. Beyond this, little controlled research on cartridge razors appears.

name: Straight razor

angle.text: Users choose the straight razor for a very close shave and the ritual of traditional wet shaving, with a smooth result that is visible right after. No studies test its effect on skin or appearance.

summary: The traditional folding open razor; popular again as a ritual and a craft, but no studies test its effect on skin or appearance.
note: Requires stropping and honing; cuts are a recognised risk for beginners.
currentQuick:
A straight razor is a single steel blade that folds into a handle. It was the standard shaving tool before safety and electric razors and has seen renewed interest since around 2008.
It is a grooming tool whose effects last until hair regrows. No clinical studies compare it with other razors.
How it works: A very sharp edge, kept aligned by stropping and sharpened by honing, slices hair at the skin surface when drawn at a shallow angle.
Risks and caveats: Nicks and cuts are the main hazards, especially for beginners. Carbon steel blades rust without care, and some blade styles are fragile or bite.
deepLead:
A straight razor, also called a cut-throat or open razor, is a single-bladed razor whose blade folds into a protective handle, known as the scales, and which is used for traditional wet shaving. Blades are made of high-carbon or stainless steel and are sharpened by the owner or a professional by honing and stropping.
Demand fell through the 20th century as safety razors and then electric razors spread, but has grown again since about 2008, with commentators citing nostalgia, long-term cost, reduced waste and craftsmanship. No clinical study of straight-razor shaving for appearance outcomes was found.

name: Shaving brush

angle.text: Wet shavers use a brush to build lather and apply it to the face, with reference works crediting it with better lather for a closer shave. The shave result is visible straight away; no trials test the brush itself.

summary: A bristle brush for lathering soap; reference works credit it with a better lather, no trials exist, and contaminated brushes caused anthrax a century ago.
note: Historical anthrax outbreaks from contaminated animal hair (1915-1924).
currentQuick:
A shaving brush builds lather from soap or cream and spreads it over the beard. Bristles come from badger, boar, horse or synthetic fibre, with silvertip badger the premium grade.
Its claimed benefits (richer lather, lifted hairs, light exfoliation) are stated in reference works; no clinical study was found.
How it works: Bristles hold water and whip soap into foam, then lift hairs while spreading it across the skin.
Risks and caveats: A 2018 historical review describes anthrax outbreaks in 1915 to 1924 from contaminated imported brushes, with about 20 percent mortality. Horse hair brushes then fell out of use for about a century.
deepLead:
A shaving brush is a handle with a tuft of bristles used to whip shaving soap or cream into lather with water and apply it to the face before shaving. Bristles are made from badger, boar, horse hair or synthetic fibre, and graded badger hair is the most prized material.
Wikipedia and Grokipedia say a brush holds water to make a richer lather, lifts facial hairs so that less razor pressure is needed, and gives mild exfoliation. No clinical study of these effects on skin or shaving outcomes was found.
The best-documented health episode is historical: between roughly 1915 and 1924, anthrax outbreaks were traced to shaving brushes made with contaminated animal hair.

name: Shaving soap / cream

angle.text: Shaving soaps, creams and gels are used to lubricate the skin so the razor glides, leaving a cleaner shave with less redness. The shave is visible immediately; the friction-reduction benefit has not been tested in trials.

summary: Lubricating soaps, creams, foams and gels for razor shaving; the aim is less friction, but no trials test it.
note: Alcohol-based and aerosol products can dry skin or be flammable.
currentQuick:
Shaving soap and cream coat the beard and skin so a razor glides with less friction. They come as bars, tubed creams, aerosol foams and gels, and have existed in some form since ancient Sumer.
Reference works describe their purpose as softer hair and less irritation, but no clinical studies were found.
How it works: Soap or surfactant, glycerine and emollients hydrate and soften hair and form a lubricating lather or film between blade and skin.
Risks and caveats: Alcohol-rich products dry the skin; aerosol cans use flammable propellants. No studies of product-specific irritation were found.
deepLead:
Shaving soap and shaving cream are lubricating products applied to the face before razor shaving to soften hair through hydration and reduce friction. Forms include hard soap bars or sticks and tubed lather creams that are worked into lather with a brush, brushless creams, aerosol foams and gels.
Grokipedia states that the products are meant to reduce nicks and irritation. No clinical trial of shaving soaps or creams for skin or appearance outcomes was found.

name: Threading kit

angle.text: Users thread eyebrows and facial hair at home for precise, clean shaping, and the result is visible immediately. It is cheap and temporary, and has been little studied.

summary: Twisted-thread plucking for brows and face: precise and cheap, temporary, barely studied.
note: Technique has little formal research; complications are rarely discussed.
currentQuick:
Threading uses a twisted thread to pull rows of fine hairs out at the follicle, mostly to shape eyebrows and clean up facial hair. A kit lets people try the technique at home.
It is an old technique with a long salon tradition. Hair grows back, so results are temporary, and published research is limited to a review of its complications.
How it works: A doubled, twisted thread is rolled across the skin, trapping hairs and lifting them out at the root in quick succession.
Risks and caveats: Pain, skin irritation and other complications have been described in a dermatology review. No formal trials compare it with waxing or tweezing.
deepLead:
Threading is a hair-removal method, used mainly on eyebrows and facial hair, in which a doubled and twisted cotton or polyester thread is rolled over unwanted hair so that it is pulled out at the follicle . A threading kit is the consumer version of the tool: thread (sometimes with a handle or tensioning aid) that allows the technique to be tried at home rather than at a salon.
The technique is described as an ancient practice that originated in the Middle East and South Asia and later spread to Western countries . It is typically performed in three ways, with the thread held by hand, by mouth or around the neck, and the mouth method is described as the fastest and most precise .
Published research is thin. A 2009 review in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology discussed the procedure's popularity and its "seldom-discussed complications" , and no controlled trials comparing threading with waxing or tweezing appear in the available literature. Results are temporary, as with other forms of epilation.

name: Sugaring paste

angle.text: Sugar paste is used as a gentler alternative to wax to remove body and facial hair, leaving smooth skin that is visible right after. It is classed as epilation in the medical literature; head-to-head trials against wax are lacking.

summary: Sugar-lemon paste that pulls hair out like wax; popular as a gentler alternative, with no head-to-head trials.
note: Some products sold as sugar wax contain wax; claims vs waxing are untested.
currentQuick:
Sugaring paste is a sugar-based substance spread on skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. Fans prefer it to wax because it is water-soluble and can be used at lower temperatures.
It is a temporary method like other epilation. Claims of less pain and fewer broken hairs are widespread but have not been tested in published comparisons.
How it works: The paste adheres to hair and is flicked or stripped off, pulling hairs out with their roots.
Risks and caveats: Skin irritation is possible, especially on sensitive skin. Reviews note limited evidence on risks and that studies mostly cover dark hair and fair skin.
deepLead:
Sugaring paste is a sticky mixture, traditionally of sugar, water and lemon juice, applied to the skin and removed to pull out hair, and is marketed as an alternative to wax . Sugaring is classed in the medical literature as a form of epilation, grouped with plucking, threading, waxing, lasers and electrolysis .
Proponents say the paste grips hair rather than skin, is water-soluble and can be used at room temperature or lightly warmed . Sugaring is also reported as one of the methods used for pubic hair removal . The published literature contains reviews of hair removal generally but no trials that specifically compare sugaring with waxing.

name: Hair-growth inhibitor lotion

angle.text: Users apply inhibitor lotions after shaving or waxing to slow regrowth of unwanted facial or body hair. The prescription ingredient eflornithine has trial data; over-the-counter versions have little.

summary: Lotions that slow hair regrowth: one Rx ingredient (eflornithine) has trial data, OTC versions have little.
note: Effect reverses after stopping; OTC formulations vary and are unstudied here.
currentQuick:
These lotions aim to slow how fast unwanted hair comes back. The prescription version, eflornithine cream, is used for facial hair in women and has clinical data behind it.
Over-the-counter retardant lotions are a loose category with varied ingredients, and no trials of them were found.
How it works: Eflornithine blocks an enzyme (ornithine decarboxylase) in the follicle, which slows hair growth rather than removing hair.
Risks and caveats: Acne, stinging, itching and rash are reported with eflornithine. Hair regrows to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping.
deepLead:
Hair-growth inhibitor lotions are topical products marketed to slow the regrowth of unwanted body or facial hair, usually after shaving, waxing or plucking. The term covers both a prescription cream and over-the-counter lotions sold as retardants.
The best documented active ingredient is eflornithine, an inhibitor of the enzyme ornithine decarboxylase, sold as a prescription cream for facial hair in women . Wikipedia reports that in clinical studies 81% of women showed improvement after twelve months, that the effect begins around eight weeks, and that hair returns to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping . Evidence for over-the-counter retardant lotions is not available in the sources reviewed.

name: Whitening toothpaste

angle.text: Users brush with whitening toothpaste to lift surface stains from coffee and tea for a brighter-looking smile within weeks. It lightens surface stain rather than the tooth's natural shade, and is a low-cost alternative to professional bleaching.

summary: Everyday toothpaste with stain-lifting extras: it lightens surface stain in weeks, not the tooth's natural shade.
note: Highly abrasive formulas can wear enamel; effect stops when use stops.
currentQuick:
Whitening toothpaste uses polishing agents, stain-loosening chemicals, sometimes peroxide or a blue pigment, to make teeth look lighter.
A systematic review cited by Wikipedia found nearly all such products reduce surface stain, but they do not change the natural colour of the tooth.
How it works: Mostly mechanical and chemical removal of surface stains, with some products adding peroxide or optical pigments.
Risks and caveats: Abrasivity (measured as RDA) can wear enamel with excessive use; peroxide products can demineralise teeth at high concentrations.
deepLead:
Whitening toothpaste is toothpaste marketed to make teeth look lighter, using mild abrasives, chemical stain-loosening agents, in some products peroxide, or optical agents such as blue covarine . It is widely sold over the counter as a low-cost alternative to professional bleaching.
Research and reference sources generally describe the effect as removal or masking of surface (extrinsic) stains rather than a change in the natural tooth colour. Wikipedia reports that daily use typically takes two to four weeks to produce visible lightening and that a 2017 systematic review found nearly all whitening dentifrices reduced extrinsic stain . A 2025 randomised crossover trial examined blue covarine toothpastes and tooth colour .

name: Mandibular advancement device

angle.text: Looksmaxxers with snoring or sleep apnea use these splints to keep the airway open and sleep better, which feeds into a rested look. It is a medical device with proven use for snoring and apnea and no published research on appearance.

summary: A jaw-forward sleep splint for snoring and apnea: a medical device with no appearance evidence.
note: Medical sleep device; can permanently change the bite.
currentQuick:
A mandibular advancement device is a custom mouthpiece worn at night that pushes the lower jaw forward to keep the airway open.
Its evidence is for sleep apnea and snoring. No studies in the sources reviewed examine it for appearance.
How it works: Holding the lower jaw forward widens the airway behind the tongue during sleep.
Risks and caveats: Dry mouth, tooth and jaw soreness and lasting changes in how the teeth meet are reported; it is a prescription device.
deepLead:
A mandibular advancement device (MAD) is a custom-made oral appliance worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward, used mainly to treat snoring and obstructive sleep apnea . It is a medical device rather than a cosmetic one, and the sources reviewed describe no published research on appearance effects.
Reviews describe CPAP as the recommended first-line treatment for obstructive sleep apnea, with MADs among alternatives that have promising data but limited strong evidence . Wikipedia reports that professional sleep societies recommend MADs for primary snoring and for people who cannot tolerate CPAP . A randomised trial has compared a MAD against CPAP in severe obstructive sleep apnea , and a systematic review has examined how device design affects outcomes .

name: Orthodontic retainer

angle.text: Retainers are worn after braces or aligners to keep teeth straight, protecting the smile people paid to straighten. Retention is well established; claims that they stunt forward growth or can expand the palate with mewing are untested.

summary: The post-braces appliance that keeps teeth where they were moved; proven for retention, untested for jaw growth.
note: Bonded wires can cause unintended tooth movement; no evidence it changes facial growth.
currentQuick:
A retainer holds teeth in place after braces or aligners, either as a removable plastic or wire device or a wire bonded behind the teeth.
Its evidence is for keeping teeth aligned. Forum claims that retainers help or block jaw and palate growth have not been studied.
How it works: Passive pressure or a bonded wire keeps teeth from drifting back while surrounding fibres adapt.
Risks and caveats: Poor hygiene can cause decay or gum inflammation; bonded retainers can cause unwanted tooth movement (wire syndrome); removable ones can break or warp.
deepLead:
An orthodontic retainer is a custom appliance, either removable (wire-and-acrylic Hawley or clear vacuum-formed plastic) or fixed (a wire bonded behind the front teeth), worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their new positions . Its purpose is to limit relapse, the tendency of teeth to drift back, which is attributed to periodontal fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure, occlusion and continued growth .
Reviews of the orthodontic literature emphasise that retention should be planned in advance, may vary in duration, and depends on patient compliance . In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are discussed mainly in relation to whether wearing or stopping them affects jaw, palate or facial growth, a claim for which the sources reviewed contain no supporting studies.

name: Palatal expander

angle.text: Palatal expanders are used mainly in children to widen the upper jaw, and some adults hope they will widen the face and improve structure, sometimes alongside mewing. Orthodontic use in kids is well supported; facial change in adults is largely untested.

summary: Screw-driven upper-jaw widener with solid orthodontic use in kids; adult facial-change claims are largely untested.
note: Relapse is common; expected benefit depends on age and type.
currentQuick:
A palatal expander widens the upper jaw by turning a screw in a fixed device, usually in children, to correct crossbites and crowding. MARPE and surgical versions exist for older patients.
Orthodontic trials support dental effects in children. Claims that expanders reshape the adult face or widen the mandible have not been tested in the sources reviewed.
How it works: Daily or weekly screw turns separate the two halves of the palate; new bone fills the gap and a retention period follows.
Risks and caveats: Speech changes, pain, a gap between front teeth, bone thinning and relapse are reported; MARPE and SARPE involve implants or surgery.
deepLead:
A palatal expander is an orthodontic device used to widen the upper jaw so that upper and lower teeth fit together better, most commonly in children and adolescents aged about 8 to 18 . Types include rapid maxillary expansion (RME), slow expansion, mini-implant-assisted expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) .
Orthodontic indications include a narrow upper jaw relative to the lower, posterior crossbite, cleft palate and crowding . In looksmaxxing communities, expanders and MARPE are discussed as ways to widen the palate or change the face, often alongside mewing. Published trials focus on dental and airway outcomes in children, and evidence for broader facial change in adults is not established in the sources reviewed.

name: Orthodontic headgear / facemask

angle.text: Headgear and facemasks are used in children to correct bite and guide jaw growth, and some looksmaxxers ask about them for a more forward midface. Evidence is in growing patients; adult facial change claims, including with MARPE or peptides, are untested.

summary: Strap-on orthodontic force appliance for kids' bite and jaw growth; adult facial-change claims lack support.
note: Compliance-dependent; eye-injury and airway concerns reported.
currentQuick:
Headgear and facemasks apply outside-the-mouth force to guide jaw growth and correct bites in children, with the facemask pulling the upper jaw forward for underbites.
Trials support use in growing patients. Looksmaxxing claims of forward maxillary growth in adults are not backed by the sources reviewed.
How it works: Straps anchor to the head or neck, and elastics or a frame transmit force to the teeth and jaw, restraining or advancing the upper jaw.
Risks and caveats: Eye injuries, tooth soreness, social stigma and possible airway or facial-growth effects are reported; effectiveness depends on many hours of daily wear.
deepLead:
Orthodontic headgear is an appliance worn partly outside the mouth, anchored by straps to the head or neck, that applies force to the teeth or jaws to correct the bite and guide growth, mainly in children . A reverse-pull headgear or facemask rests on the forehead and chin and uses elastics to pull the upper jaw forward, and is used for underbites .
The Cochrane review of orthodontic treatment for Class III malocclusion in children describes the facemask as the most commonly reported non-surgical intervention, usually attached to an expansion appliance . In looksmaxxing communities, facemasks combined with MARPE are discussed as a non-surgical route to forward maxillary growth, a claim for which published support concerns children rather than adults.

name: Herbst / twin-block functional appliance

angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances are used in growing teens with an overbite to bring the lower jaw forward, improving the side profile. Research shows modest lower-jaw gain mostly in children; use outside the Class II indication or with home-made substitutes is untested.

summary: Orthodontic jaw-advancement appliances for growing teens with an overbite; research shows modest lower-jaw gain, mostly in children.
note: Studied in growing patients with Class II malocclusion; no studies as an adult aesthetic treatment.
currentQuick:
The Herbst (fixed) and Twin Block (removable) are orthodontic appliances that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children and teenagers with an overbite. Orthodontists prescribe them to correct the bite.
In looksmaxxing forums they are discussed as a way to advance a small or recessed lower jaw. Trials and meta-analyses report a modest average gain in lower-jaw length, around 1.5 to 2 mm or more versus controls, together with tooth movement.
How it works: The appliance posture the lower jaw forward. Orthodontists describe the result as a mix of tooth movement, bone adaptation and possible extra lower-jaw growth or joint remodelling, with debate over how much is skeletal.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include early soreness and chewing difficulty, speech changes with removable plates, and forward tilting of lower front teeth. The appliances are fitted by orthodontists for growing patients. Forum claims that they recess the upper jaw are not borne out by a 2022 meta-analysis of upper-jaw position.
deepLead:
The Herbst appliance and the Twin Block appliance are orthodontic devices known as functional appliances. They are used in growing children and adolescents with a Class II malocclusion, in which the upper front teeth sit forward of the lower ones and the lower jaw is often small or set back relative to the upper jaw. The Herbst is fixed to the teeth and holds the lower jaw forward through telescoping rods, while the Twin Block is a removable pair of acrylic plates that guide the lower jaw forward when the patient bites together. 
Systematic reviews generally report that functional appliances correct overjet and molar relationship in growing patients, with a mix of tooth movement and skeletal change. A review of mandibular changes found that about two-thirds of the studied samples showed more than 2 mm of supplementary lower-jaw lengthening compared with untreated controls, with larger effects when treatment coincided with the pubertal growth period.  A meta-analysis comparing the two appliances reported slightly greater mandibular body lengthening with the Herbst.
